DISPLAY_WIDTH.doc:
Display widths: how many columns of a terminal a code point takes.

A terminal gives a character one column, or two for the wide characters
of East Asian scripts and for emoji, or none for a mark that combines
with the character before it. The widths come from the Unicode Character
Database (East Asian Width, the general categories, emoji presentation)
of the version `version`, by tables that scripts/gen-unicode-tables.py
makes. Characters of ambiguous East Asian width are one column, as
terminals outside East Asian locales show them. What is shown of a
grapheme cluster as a whole -- an emoji joined to another, a flag -- is
`Grapheme.width`'s.

members.name: version
members.doc:
The version of Unicode the tables are made from.

**Example** `version = "18.0.0"`

members.name: codePoint
members.doc:
`codePoint c` is the columns `c` takes on a terminal: 0, 1 or 2.

It is 0 for a nonspacing, enclosing or format mark and for the medial
vowels and final consonants of conjoining Hangul; 2 for an East Asian
wide or fullwidth character and for an emoji shown as one by default;
1 for the rest. A control character is 0 too: a program shows it its
own way (`isControl`).

**Example** `codePoint 0x61 = 1 andalso codePoint 0x6F22 = 2 andalso codePoint 0x301 = 0 andalso codePoint 0x1F600 = 2`

members.name: isControl
members.doc:
`isControl c` is whether `c` is a control character, of C0 (below
0x20, and 0x7F) or of C1 (0x80 to 0x9F).

**Example** `isControl 0x1B andalso not (isControl 0x20)`

members.name: columns
members.doc:
`columns s` is the columns the UTF-8 of `s` takes, the sum of the
widths of its code points; an ill-formed part counts as the
replacement character, one column.

**Example** `columns "a\230\188\162" = 3`

GRAPHEME.doc:
Grapheme clusters: the characters a reader sees, by the rules of Unicode
Standard Annex \#29.

A user-perceived character may be several code points: a letter and the
accents on it, a Hangul syllable of conjoining jamo, an Indic conjunct,
an emoji with a skin tone or joined to others by U+200D, a flag of two
regional indicators. An editor moves its cursor and deletes by extended
grapheme cluster, and a terminal draws one cluster in one cell or two.
The rules are those of the Annex for the version `version` of Unicode;
the test data of that version (GraphemeBreakTest.txt) passes.

members.name: version
members.doc:
The version of Unicode whose rules and properties are followed.

**Example** `version = "18.0.0"`

members.name: next
members.doc:
`next (s, i)` is the offset just past the extended grapheme cluster
that begins at byte `i` of `s`. An ill-formed part of the UTF-8 is a
cluster of its own.

**Raises** `Subscript` unless `0 <= i` and `i < size s`.

**Example** `next ("e\204\129x", 0) = 3`

members.name: clusters
members.doc:
`clusters s` is the clusters of `s`, in order.

**Example** `clusters "e\204\129x" = ["e\204\129", "x"]`

members.name: count
members.doc:
`count s` is how many clusters `s` has.

**Example** `count "\240\159\135\179\240\159\135\177" = 1`, a flag

members.name: policy
members.doc:
How a terminal measures a cluster: as one, or as its code points.

Windows Terminal and kitty measure a cluster as one, as Unicode
recommends; xterm, and VS Code's terminal by report, add up its code
points.

members.name: width
members.doc:
`width policy s` is the columns `s` takes on a terminal that measures
by `policy`.

**Example** `width ByCluster "\240\159\145\169\226\128\141\240\159\145\167" = 2`

**Example** `width ByCodePoint "\240\159\145\169\226\128\141\240\159\145\167" = 4`

UTF8.doc:
UTF-8: code points written as bytes and read back, strictly.

A string holds bytes, and text in it is UTF-8 by convention. Reading is
strict in the sense of the Unicode Standard (its section 3.9): an
overlong form, a surrogate, a code point past 0x10FFFF, a sequence cut
short and a continuation byte with no lead are ill-formed, and `decode`
gives `NONE` for them. Where a program must read whatever bytes it gets
\-- what a terminal sends, a file of unknown origin -- `next` and the
functions over whole strings never fail: they read each ill-formed part
as one replacement character, U+FFFD, as long as the maximal subpart the
standard recommends, so that the same bytes give the same characters in
every program that follows it.

members.name: replacement
members.doc:
The replacement character, U+FFFD, which the readers that never fail
give for each ill-formed part.

**Example** `replacement = 0xFFFD`

members.name: isScalar
members.doc:
`isScalar c` is whether `c` is a Unicode scalar value, a code point
that UTF-8 can write: from 0 to 0x10FFFF, and not a surrogate (0xD800
to 0xDFFF).

**Example** `isScalar 0x10FFFF andalso not (isScalar 0xD800)`

members.name: encode
members.doc:
`encode c` is the bytes of the code point `c`: one for ASCII, up to
four.

**Raises** `Chr` if `c` is not a scalar value.

**Example** `encode 0x20AC = "\226\130\172"`

members.name: decode
members.spec: val decode : string * int -> (int * int) option
members.doc:
`decode (s, i)` is the code point whose bytes begin at byte `i` of
`s`, and how many bytes it has; `NONE` when the bytes there are
ill-formed, or `i` is the end of `s`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i > size s`.

**Example** `decode ("\226\130\172", 0) = SOME (0x20AC, 3)`

**Example** `decode ("\192\128", 0) = NONE`, an overlong form of 0

members.name: next
members.spec: val next : string * int -> int * int
members.doc:
`next (s, i)` is the code point at byte `i` of `s` and its length, or
`replacement` where the bytes there are ill-formed.

A well-formed code point is what `decode` gives; an ill-formed part is
as long as its maximal subpart.

**Raises** `Subscript` unless `0 <= i` and `i < size s`.

**Example** `next ("\240\128\128", 0) = (0xFFFD, 1)`

members.name: isValid
members.doc:
`isValid s` is whether all of `s` is well-formed UTF-8.

**Example** `isValid "caf\195\169" andalso not (isValid "\237\160\128")`

members.name: explode
members.doc:
`explode s` is the code points of `s`, read by `next`.

**Law** `implode (explode s) = s` when `isValid s`

**Example** `explode "a\195\169\255" = [0x61, 0xE9, 0xFFFD]`

members.name: implode
members.doc:
`implode cs` is the bytes of the code points `cs`, one after another.

**Raises** `Chr` if one of `cs` is not a scalar value.

**Law** `explode (implode cs) = cs` when `List.all isScalar cs`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init s` is `f` applied to the code points of `s` from the
left, read by `next`, starting from `init`.

**Example** `foldl (fn (c, n) => c + n) 0 "\195\169" = 0xE9`

members.name: size
members.doc:
`size s` is the number of code points of `s`, read by `next`.

**Example** `size "caf\195\169" = 4`
